planting.note: Plant rooted semi-hardwood cuttings or container stock in spring, ideally tucked at the base of large rocks that shade the root zone through hot afternoons.

directions: Waxflower is a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub of rocky slopes and canyon walls across the central and southern Rockies, where it tucks into the dappled light at the base of boulders and aspen groves. In late spring it opens dense, intensely fragrant clusters of waxy white flowers, followed in fall by brilliant orange and burgundy foliage and flaking cinnamon-colored bark that adds winter interest. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer, since seed is slow and unreliable, and set plants where afternoon shade shields the shallow roots from heat. Once established it needs only occasional supplemental water, making it a durable choice for dry, partially shaded slopes that most shrubs find inhospitable.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in fall or spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath conifers or aspens; growth is slow, so avoid disturbing the roots once sited.

directions: Mountain lover is a low, mounding evergreen shrub of montane and subalpine conifer forests from British Columbia to New Mexico, where its glossy, boxwood-like leaves persist through deep snow and dense shade. Tiny maroon flowers appear along the stems in late spring but are easy to overlook; the real value is the plant's year-round structure in dry shade where few other natives thrive. Grow from rooted cuttings taken in late fall or winter, since seed propagation is slow and seldom used commercially, and set plants in humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath pines, firs, or aspens. Established plants tolerate drought well and spread slowly to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Surface-sow seed in fall so winter cold and moisture break dormancy naturally, or replicate the cycle indoors with a warm period followed by six weeks of moist cold stratification before moving to a bright, cool spot.

directions: Showy Jacob's ladder is a compact, mounding perennial of rocky subalpine slopes and open forest edges throughout the Rocky Mountain high country, prized for its finely divided, skunky-scented foliage and clusters of blue to lavender, yellow-throated flowers. Surface-sow seed in fall so winter cold and moisture break dormancy naturally, or mimic the cycle indoors with several weeks at room temperature followed by a cold, moist spell in the refrigerator before moving seed trays to a cool, bright location. It performs best in gritty, fast-draining soil tucked among rocks where it receives morning sun and afternoon shade, conditions that mimic its native talus and forest-margin habitat. Deadheading spent flower stalks encourages a longer summer bloom period and limits self-seeding in smaller rock gardens.
sources: British Columbia Ministry of Forests Native Seed Manual

planting.note: Plant rooted semi-hardwood cuttings or container stock in spring into lean, rocky, well-drained soil; wedge among stones for the drainage and cool root zone it needs.

directions: Rock spirea is a loosely arching, rock-crevice shrub of the southern and central Rockies and Great Basin, where it roots into shallow soil pockets on cliff faces and talus slopes in part shade. Feathery plumes of small white to pink flowers cover the arching branches in mid-summer, followed by persistent tan seed clusters and vivid fall color in shades of orange, red, and purple. Because its tiny seeds need months of cold, moist stratification and germinate unreliably, most gardeners establish plants from semi-hardwood cuttings or purchased container stock rather than from seed. It thrives in lean, rocky, well-drained soil and needs little water once established, making it a good companion for other dry-shade natives at the base of rock outcrops.

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors in fall so winter cold breaks seed dormancy, or divide established clumps in spring or fall; seedlings are slow and may take several years to reach flowering size.

directions: Wyoming kittentails is a low, clump-forming perennial of montane and subalpine grasslands and open conifer forests across the central Rockies and northern Great Plains, where woolly gray-green basal leaves emerge before the snow is fully gone. In spring, dense spikes of small purple, petal-less flowers rise just above the foliage, giving the plant its common name and attracting some of the season's earliest bees. Divide established clumps in spring or fall, or sow seed outdoors in autumn so winter cold breaks dormancy naturally, since seedlings are slow to reach flowering size. Plant in gritty, well-drained soil at the lightly shaded edge of aspen or conifer stands, where it tolerates both summer drought and harsh mountain winters.
sources: Montana Field Guide (Montana Natural Heritage Program)

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or container stock in fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; avoid sites near five-needle pines because of white pine blister rust.

directions: Whitestem gooseberry is a nearly thornless, arching shrub found along streambanks and in moist, partially shaded forest understory from British Columbia south through the Rocky Mountain states, where it forms loose thickets at the forest edge. Small greenish to maroon-tinged flowers hang from the branches in spring, maturing into smooth purple-black berries that are tart but edible fresh or cooked into jam. Propagate from dormant hardwood or semi-ripe cuttings taken in winter or late summer, since seed requires months of cold stratification and germinates slowly and unevenly. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and avoid planting near five-needle pines, since Ribes species can host white pine blister rust.
